stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the study casts doubt on?
stimulus: Seismologists long thought that frequent small earthquakes along a fault release built-up stress, making a large earthquake on that fault less likely. However, a 2024 study of 300 faults found that large earthquakes were just as common on faults with many small quakes as on faults with few, casting doubt on the idea that ______
choices: small earthquakes lower the chance of a large earthquake on the same fault.
large earthquakes occur equally often on faults with many or few small quakes.
small earthquakes are what trigger large earthquakes on the same fault.
seismologists have now gathered data on roughly 300 faults worldwide.
explanation: The blank comes right after 'casting doubt on the idea that,' so it has to restate the old view: the one before 'However.' Seismologists thought small quakes release stress and make big ones less likely. The study's result (big quakes are just as common either way) attacks that exact reasoning, so A is the idea being doubted. This is the first step of every 'new evidence undercuts a prior view' inference question: find the old view and put it in the blank.

B.why: This is what the new study found, which puts it on the wrong side of 'However.' Evidence can't cast doubt on itself. You picked the finding when the blank asked for the belief the finding overturns.

C.why: The study showed that small quakes don't make large ones less likely. It never tested whether small quakes cause large ones. You flipped the old view into its opposite and treated that as something the passage discusses.

D.why: This is about the study's sample size, a background detail. It isn't a view that anyone held or that the evidence could undercut.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the measurements cast doubt on?
stimulus: Many hydrologists have assumed that the amount of water a mountain stream carries in summer depends mainly on how much rain falls that summer. But measurements from 40 mountain streams showed that summer flow tracked the depth of the previous winter's snowpack far more closely than it tracked summer rain, challenging the assumption that ______
choices: winter snowpack is the main source of a mountain stream's summer flow.
summer rainfall mainly determines how much water a stream carries in summer.
summer rainfall has no effect on a stream's flow in any season of the year.
hydrologists measure mountain streams more often than they measure lowland rivers.
explanation: 'Challenging the assumption that' tells you the blank holds the old assumption, which is the sentence before 'But.' Hydrologists assumed summer rain mainly drives summer flow. The measurements point to snowpack instead, and that attacks this assumption directly. Spotting which side of the contrast the blank belongs to is the skill that 'challenging the assumption' inference questions rest on.

A.why: This is what the new measurements suggest, so it sits after 'But.' You picked the evidence's conclusion when the blank wanted the assumption being challenged.

C.why: The data show that rain matters less than snowpack, not that it doesn't matter at all. 'No effect' and 'any season' are far stronger than anything the passage establishes.

D.why: The passage never compares how often different rivers are measured. This choice is about method, not the view the data undercut.

stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the observation casts doubt on?
stimulus: Astronomers once believed that a planet orbiting very close to its star could not hold on to an atmosphere, because the star's intense heat would strip any gas away. However, telescope observations of a scorching close-orbiting planet revealed a thick layer of gas surrounding it, casting doubt on the idea that ______
choices: a planet very close to its star can still keep a thick layer of gas.
every planet orbiting close to its star has a thick atmosphere of gas.
a planet very close to its star is unable to hold on to an atmosphere.
telescopes can now measure the surface temperature of distant stars.
explanation: The old view comes before 'However': astronomers believed close-orbiting planets couldn't keep an atmosphere. One close planet with a thick layer of gas is a direct counterexample to that belief, so C is the idea being doubted. In this subtype, you don't need to know any astronomy. You just restate the 'once believed' sentence.

A.why: This is what the observation shows, so it's on the 'However' side of the passage. You chose the new evidence instead of the old belief it overturns.

B.why: The observation covers one planet. Jumping to 'every planet' is strength creep: one counterexample can disprove 'none,' but it can't prove 'all.'

D.why: Measuring star temperatures is never discussed, and it isn't a view the observation could challenge. It just mentions telescopes, which is the right topic but the wrong task.

subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?

stem: Groundwork: Which choice completes the text by restating the view that the survey casts doubt on?
stimulus: Some ecologists have claimed that beaver dams harm trout populations by blocking the fish from moving up and down streams. But a survey of 25 streams found more trout in stretches above beaver dams than in comparable streams with no dams at all, casting doubt on the claim that ______
choices: streams with beaver dams tend to hold more trout than streams without them.
beaver dams improve conditions for every fish species in every stream.
ecologists have surveyed trout populations in about 25 different streams.
beaver dams harm trout populations by keeping the fish from moving freely.
explanation: The blank follows 'casting doubt on the claim that,' so it restates the claim from before 'But': beaver dams harm trout by blocking movement. Finding more trout above the dams undercuts that claim. Practicing this move, matching the blank to the old claim, unlocks the 'what does the new evidence cast doubt on?' inference question.

A.why: This restates what the survey found, which is the side after 'But.' The survey can't cast doubt on its own result. That's the subtype's main trap.

B.why: The survey counted only trout. 'Every fish species in every stream' goes far beyond what was measured, and the passage never says dams improve anything.

C.why: This repeats a detail about the survey's size. It isn't a claim that anyone made or that the evidence challenges.
